book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
samples: William Irwin's editor introduction tells how a tape of "N.I.B." stopping at "My name is Lucifer, please take my hand" hooked him at thirteen, and argues Sabbath deserve serious philosophy: their riffs and lyrics confront existential despair, war, drugs, and the nature of evil in shades of gray rather than Satanism. It frames the book's guiding questions (what makes Sabbath sound evil, is evil in the ear of the beholder, is it still Sabbath without Ozzy) and promises that philosophers can deepen our listening to Ozzy, Tony, Geezer, and Bill without recovering authorial intent.

William Irwin reads the Ozzy-era catalog as unwitting British existentialism: "Johnny Blade", "Paranoid", and "Wheels of Confusion" voice Camus's absurd, the mismatch between our desires and a world where life has no meaning and "hell is other people" explains why Iron Man, saved yet treated as a mindless thing, plans vengeance. The chapter argues the band moves from despair toward freedom and self-creation: "Supernaut" and "Under the Sun" reject religion in the spirit of Nietzsche's death of God, "Cornucopia" depicts bad-faith conformity to plastic suburban lives, and "Children of the Grave" plus Sabbath's own music-making exemplify the claim that artistic creativity is the proper response to pain, with the fan invited to sculpt himself into an authentic individual Sisyphus-style.

Liz Stillwaggon Swan surveys Sabbath's pictures of moral evil (nuclear annihilation in "Electric Funeral", heroin's "deadly pin" in "Hand of Doom", social oppression allegorized as the Satan of "Black Sabbath") and argues the band poses the problem of evil without solving it theologically. Against the view that invoking evil presupposes God, she aligns Sabbath with Augustine's rejection of Manichaean evil-as-a-force, reading evil as a privation traceable to free human choices, and with Bertrand Russell's "A Free Man's Worship": "Children of the Grave", "Into the Void", "Spiral Architect", and "Symptom of the Universe" urge that we defeat evil by imagining and building a better possible reality through love, vegan-pacifist Geezer Butler being the living proof behind the stage persona.

Brian Froese argues Black Sabbath's occult imagery expresses an eschatological imagination forged in the rubble of working-class, postwar Birmingham as a rebuke to hippie utopianism. Songs like "Black Sabbath", "War Pigs" (originally "Walpurgis"), and "Electric Funeral" borrow the literary devices of the Book of Revelation, Satan, final judgment, cosmic journeys, as what Elaine Pagels calls war literature for a Cold War and Vietnam world, while "Iron Man" transvalues the Christian savior into a resurrected anti-hero and "After Forever" and "Lord of this World" both embrace and resent the faith. He concludes the band built a sacralized, contradictory, fatalistic cosmology in which "the chosen one" cannot escape his fate, reworking Christian apocalypse for the industrial marginalized.

Joel McIver, drawing on years of interviewing the band, argues the sinister sound is psychoacoustics rather than Satan: Iommi's lower tuning adopted after the sheet-metal press took his fingertips, the tritone or diabolus in musica that anchors "Black Sabbath", horror-film tremolo, minor keys, Ozzy's untrained monotone, and Bill Ward's slightly dragged, jazzy beats, artistic imperfections that keep the music lifelike. Against Schopenhauer's view that music directly expresses universal emotions, so the tritone would naturally sound like discord to anyone, McIver contends the devil's interval is a Western convention that only became inseparable from evil once Sabbath fused it with Geezer's occult lyrics and nightmare cover art.

James Heathers asks why the most improbable band became the one true originator of heavy metal and answers with Schopenhauer: industrial Aston, Birmingham was a monument to the ceaseless, unsatisfied striving of the Will, and music, which maps directly onto the Will itself, gave that world its voice. The tritone's numerically hideous ratios, a point traced through Rameau back to Pythagoras, make it the natural interval of morbidity, which is why "Black Sabbath" and everything from Liszt's Dante Sonata to death metal is marinated in it, and why doom was not a predictable development like Deep Purple or Led Zeppelin. He closes on the irony that Schopenhauer, who preached ascetic denial of the Will, would have loathed a band that answered factory-town despair by smothering the Will in lager, hash, cocaine, and women, only to breed more want in the worst of all possible worlds.

samples: Editor Jason Holt's introduction explains the 'ultimate' title and stakes the book's claim that The Daily Show is philosophically engaging, not mere late-night entertainment. He unpacks the subtitle: 'moments of Zen' are poignant closing clips that encapsulate a speaker's hypocrisy or an unsaid truth, only loosely Zen in valuing gestured rather than stated insight; 'indecision theory' fuses the show's Indecision election coverage with decision theory's study of rational political choice, since a running concern of the show is critically evaluating information sources. He then maps the book's five segments, from fake news through Stewart as philosopher figure to religion, culture, and Colbert.

Erion reads The Daily Show's sharpest bits as jokes that only work if the audience already grasps Neil Postman's thesis in Amusing Ourselves to Death that television's entertainment bias renders news irrational, irrelevant and incoherent, from hurricane-reporter parodies and 'The Less You Know' to news-style graphics like 'Mess O' Potamia'. He treats Stewart's 2004 Crossfire confrontation ('stop hurting America', 'you're doing theater, when you should be doing debate'), the 2009 Jim Cramer CNBC 'Brawl Street' interview after the financial crisis, and the 2011 Chris Wallace exchange as explicit versions of the same critique that TV's real bias is toward sensationalism, conflict and laziness rather than partisanship. He closes with the Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear's 'conflictinator' speech, noting Stewart is ultimately more optimistic than Postman that television could clarify rather than obfuscate.

Gettings asks how a self-described fake news show can inform viewers, and answers by defining fiction as non-deceptive make-believe, Stewart's 'hilarious make-'em-ups' (the Rick Santorum quiz), distinct from lies because truth-value and research do not settle the category, as when Colbert's 2003 projection of Bush's reelection accidentally came true but stayed fiction. He identifies the show's cues for separating real from fake: sheer outrageousness (Samantha Bee on North Korean soldiers), the convention of Stewart playing straight man to unreliable 'senior' correspondents (John Oliver's fabricated Truman history, Ed Helms on the John Roberts nomination), and obviously doctored graphics like Jason Jones's Clooney fundraiser photo. He then argues the show conveys general truths about government and media, using John Kyl's Planned Parenthood falsehood, CNN and Fox botching the Supreme Court's Obamacare ruling, and the Steve Cohen Nazi-comparison hypocrisy, before contrasting its news-rooted humor with The Onion's near-total invention.

Sotos locates The Daily Show within an emergent 'Fifth Estate', a watchdog for the failing Fourth Estate press, and recruits Arendt's actor/spectator distinction to defend Stewart's refusal of activism: like judge, journalist or comedian, the spectator withdraws from action yet gives events their meaning and voice in public conversation. She traces an American fake-news lineage from James and Benjamin Franklin's colonial papers (Silence Dogood, Polly Baker, the Vindex Patriae hoax) through Twain to Stewart, contrasting honest satire with Glenn Beck and Rush Limbaugh's 'fake fake news' and the repeal of the Fairness Doctrine. Juvenalian indignatio ( Stewart's somber 'Fuck you' to CNBC in the Clusterf#@k to the Poor House) and Horatian playfulness (Colbert's Super PAC saga) supply the ethos, and she reads the Rally to Restore Sanity as Aristophanic Old Comedy, complete with agon, parabasis ('A Moment of Sincerity') and a reconciliatory ending that makes 'We the People' exist.

Littmann asks how a program built on mockery, falsehoods like Wyatt Cenac's Sarah Palin jokes and the 'santorum' coinage, can be a serious political voice, situating it in the tradition running from Aristophanes' roasting of Cleon and his distorting Clouds portrait of Socrates through Juvenal to Twain. He rejects Juvenal's hope that shame reforms the mocked (people do not listen to those who disrespect them) and argues mockery's real value is keeping issues like racism, war and Glenn Beck's rhetoric in public consciousness. Deploying Mill's On Liberty arguments against censorship, that silencing assumes infallibility and truth is sharpened by collision with error, he warns mockery works like censorship when audiences dismiss mocked views without consideration, the key difference being that Limbaugh demands to be taken seriously while Stewart bills himself as a comedian, and closes with Plato's Meno: opinions must be 'shackled' by understanding why they are true, not adopted because a comedy laughed at the alternative.

Bean reads both fake-news shows through Baudrillard's account of a media age with 'more and more information and less and less meaning': mainstream news is already simulation, and Colbert is 'a walking talking simulacrum', more O'Reilly than O'Reilly, whose five-deep receding portrait series and 'The Wørd' graphics (the abstinence-education 'Gateway Hug' bit) stage signs that refer only to themselves. Stewart, broadcasting from a simulacrum of a simulacrum, a television news studio, instead punctures the hyperreal: translating Obama's 'audacity of hope' convention speech into 'calibration of expectations' and rendering Laura Ingraham's dismissal of the party platform in Valley Girl vocal fry. Adapting Baudrillard's fake-holdup thought experiment into an 'organize a fake news broadcast' test, she argues the shows fall into the real precisely because they report on and stage simulation, anchoring audiences against media's 'communication without a response'.

book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
essays: Might God Be Hidden for Love's Sake
“Cogs that Fit, that Cooperate by Design”
What We Have Learned, or “Always Let Your Conscience Be Your Guide!”
Where Do We Go from Here
Rafiki Holds the Mirror Up to Nature
He’ll Be There For You, No Matter What
Changing Fate or Being Changed by Fate
We Can Fix this Hand in Hand
The Rhythm by Which We Live Our Lives
samples: Editor Richard B. Davis frames the whole volume with Socrates' claim that philosophy begins in wonder, arguing that the Disney universe of films and theme parks is a fitting place to ask who we are, what our purpose is, and how we can live freely and happily. He previews the book's arcs: the feminist evolution of the princesses from Snow White to Moana, whether Hidden Mickeys tell us anything about God, and journeys through Inside Out's emotions and Finding Dory's disability stigmas.

Reads The Little Mermaid as a step forward from the man-requiring damsels of Snow White and Sleeping Beauty: Ariel reverses the rescue by saving Eric, and Aristotle's 'all men by nature desire to know' is stretched to cover her curiosity about the human world. But Ursula's bargain trading Ariel's voice for legs dramatizes the long history of silenced women (Eve, Pandora, Cassandra, the scold's bridle), and the film's sexy, silent Ariel is exactly what Mulvey's male gaze, built on Sartre's 'the look,' criticizes. Applying Beauvoir's 'one is not born but becomes a woman,' the chapter argues Ariel shows biology is not destiny yet still regresses into needing a man, concluding she is a flawed but real advance toward better heroines.

Argues that Disney's Mulan transplants a distinctly modern Western ideal of the authentic self ('true to your heart,' 'Reflection') into a Confucian honor culture where the self is constituted by roles and relationships, filial piety (xiao), and ren as the virtue that binds people into larger wholes — which is why the film flopped in China. The matchmaker debacle, Fa Zhou's 'I will die doing what's right,' and the family's shame show a culture where dishonor stains the whole family and even luck (the cricket Cri-Kee) fixes moral standing, conflicting with Western assumptions about individual responsibility. The chapter ends by noting Mulan now resonates with young Chinese viewers, asking whether the Western individualist self is a truth about humanity or a cultural export that, like the Huns, has scaled the Great Wall.

Sets up Disney's maxim 'Hey kid, you can be a hero' as the direct opposite of Zen's 'Hey kid, you can be a buddha': escapism versus liberation, told through the life of Dogen, whose monastic choice parallels Disney hero narratives. Mickey in Steamboat Willie — a bundle of still frames with no sound and no real 'he' — illustrates the Buddha's three marks of existence (emptiness, impermanence, frustration), and the chapter argues Disney products are calibrated distractions from these marks while Dogen counsels facing them, with Ariel's Andersen fate as the price of fantasy. It closes on Disney's merchandising machine (Yoda, Star Wars sequels, direct-to-video cash grabs) as everything the countercultural minimalist Yoda or Baloo's bare necessities stand against, concluding that real hakuna matata is accepting impermanence rather than escaping it.

Uses Hidden Mickeys — like the ambiguous log-and-dump-truck at the Once Upon a Toy store — to attack the first premise of Schellenberg's argument from divine hiddenness: just as an arrangement of shapes can be a deliberate Hidden Mickey or a decorative accident, so God's traces in the world can be genuinely ambiguous, letting a non-resistant non-believer rationally fail to believe. Mother Teresa's decades of felt abandonment and C. S. Lewis's 'door slammed in the face' from A Grief Observed frame the experiential problem, and the authors concede the disanalogy that we independently know agents run Disney but not that God exists. As a partial response they offer Lewis's Screwtape suggestion that 'He cannot ravish, He can only woo': God hides precisely so that love can be freely given.

Reads the government ban on Supers in The Incredibles through Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration and Mill's On Liberty, arguing the ban rests on the 'PREFER' principle — society's likings and dislikings as law — fed by perception management (Winston Deavor's suit-cameras PR campaign) rather than reasons, just as Locke diagnosed intolerance, not diversity of opinion, as the cause of civil strife. Mill's harm principle, illustrated by Elastigirl's 'drinking on duty' remark, should instead govern, so banning Supers' powers and pressuring Dash to suppress his speed ('Everyone's special, Dash' / 'Which is another way of saying no one is') is tyranny. Mr. Huph's 'cogs that fit, that cooperate by design' image of Insuricare shows the conformist cost: a society built on preference rather than reasons will never produce great thinkers.

book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
essays: The Existential Redefinition of Doctor Strange
We Can All Be Socratics Supreme
I Control It by Surrendering Control
One Thing We Know Is That Life Is Strange
We’ve Run Out of Time… or Have We
Knock and the Door Will Be Opened… Eventually
By the Crimson Bands of Cyttorak… We Conclude!
samples: The introduction surveys Doctor Strange's history from Stan Lee and Steve Ditko's 1963 comics to the 2016 Benedict Cumberbatch film, framing him as Marvel's mystic loner defended by Wong and trained by the Ancient One. It previews the book's guiding philosophical questions: how Strange reconciles hard-boiled science with mystical training, why his line about being 'tiny momentary specks within an indifferent universe' was wrong, what his astral self says about mind and body, and why he is always so alone.

Dunn argues that Strange begins as a foot soldier of the Baconian project (Bacon and Descartes' program of conquering nature and treating death as an enemy to be subdued, embodied in his surgical God-complex and neurogenesis research), and that its shipwreck drives him to Kamar-Taj. Using Nietzsche, he reads both Strange and Kaecilius as sick with the 'spirit of revenge against time' — Kaecilius fleeing into Dormammu's timeless Dark Dimension as Nietzsche's Hinterweltler, Strange clinging to his unrecoverable past. The climactic 'Dormammu, I've come to bargain' time loop is interpreted as Nietzsche's eternal return weaponized, and Strange's 'Pain's an old friend' as his achievement of amor fati, echoing the Ancient One's dying claim that death is what gives life meaning.

Lee reads Strange's car crash as Heideggerian angst and the Call of conscience that ends his 'ontic' life of treating patients as reputation-building problems, forcing a choice between authenticity and a mask. Kaecilius and Dormammu embody the inauthentic flight from death (Kaecilius going 'beyond good and evil' Nietzsche-style), while the Ancient One's confession — drawing on the Dark Dimension only until Strange could replace her, then stretching one moment into a thousand to watch the snow — models accepting mortality. Dormammu's torment in Strange's time loop is compared to Camus's Sisyphus, supporting the thesis that without an ending life is endless repetition, so 'death gives meaning to life.'

Cleary reads Strange as a would-be Nietzschean Übermensch — brilliant, striving, and flirting with nihilism via the 'tiny momentary speck' line — whose narcissism, not his ideals, blocks both self-overcoming and love. Strange's rage at Christine Palmer's wine and cheese ('don't pity me') is explained through Nietzsche's attack on pity as herd morality, and his fixation on restoring his old surgeon-self as refusing Zarathustra's call to burn oneself to ashes. The Ancient One leaving him to die on Everest, Mordo's hard training, and Wong refusing to laugh at his jokes exemplify Nietzschean friendship as challenge and 'war,' culminating in the 'shared higher thirst for an ideal above them' that lets Strange overcome himself.

DiGeorgio traces Strange's 'existential conversion' from scientific nihilism ('matter and nothing more') through Sartrean bad faith — playing the brilliant surgeon while not really believing life meaningless, refusing the Ancient One's widened keyhole — to authenticity. His hesitation to stay and fight after killing a zealot, and the Ancient One's 'it's not about you,' set up his choice to defend humanity as Sartre's universal decree, choosing for all humankind in anguish and freedom. The endless time loop imposed on Dormammu is read as Nietzsche's eternal recurrence demanding total commitment to one's choices, so that by the end Strange lives existence-precedes-essence: what he does, not his 'brilliant surgeon' essence, defines him.

Boudreaux maps Strange's comic-book journey into the Orb of Agamotto (dragged in by the Silver Dagger, greeted by a hookah-smoking caterpillar, tempted by counterfeit heroes like the Silver Surfer and Hulk) onto Descartes's Meditations. Empiricism (Locke's tabula rasa, Hume's sense-data) collapses when the senses are so thoroughly deceived inside the Orb, and innate ideas plus the Law of Non-Contradiction are not enough, so Strange reasons his way to the cogito — 'Nothing merits belief here — except oneself!' — just as Descartes doubts the evil demon. The caterpillar is revealed as Agamotto, playing the role of Descartes's non-deceiving God whose guidance lets Strange escape, and Strange's astral projections are offered as dramatic proof of mind-body dualism.

book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
essays: 1. Finding the Meaning of Life in Downton Abbey
2. I May Be a Socialist, But I’m Not a Lunatic
4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful
8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word
10. Does Bates Know Who Raped Anna
12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys
13. Topophilia; or, How We Got Hooked on Downton
14. Things Can Happen that Nobody Could Imagine Only a Few Years Ago
15. Memories. In the End, Is That All There Is
16. Female Integrity in Times of Change
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Downton's quaint domestic plots burst with universal moral and social meaning beneath their surface. Using the season 1 snuffbox incident, in which Thomas frames the innocent Bates for theft, it shows how the episode stages archetypal villainy and innocence akin to the universal figures of Plato's Republic and world mythology, so the 'simple' plot is morally clear rather than superficial. It then reads the hierarchy of Thomas, Bates, and Lord Grantham through Confucian propriety and Aristotelian justice, suggesting that justice partly consists in attention to 'greater and lesser,' something Western viewers raised on equality find foreign yet intriguing. Finally it insists that as concrete persons all three are morally mixed (Thomas takes a beating to spare Jimmy, Bates may have killed outside the law, Grantham is generous to tenants but cold to his daughters), and that this complexity is what rewards philosophical reflection, along with Hume's 'small morals' of etiquette.

Blessing pits Steve Jobs's 'Do What You Love' creed (and Oprah's 'follow your bliss') against Downton's world of inherited roles, where nobody from Anna to Lady Mary chooses their work. She distinguishes happiness from meaningfulness, since Matthew's war wounds and Mary's grief over his death are painful yet deeply meaningful, and tests subjectivist theories such as Nietzsche's meaning-as-passionate-process against Nozick's demand that a meaningful life leave permanent traces and Susan Wolf's hybrid 'loving objects that are worthy of love.' Kant's duty to develop one's talents rather than idle for pleasure, and Lord Grantham's self-description as 'a custodian, not an owner,' anchor the show's counter-ethos of duty over desire, embodied in Carson, Mrs. Hughes, and Mrs. Patmore's pride in unloved, socially necessary work. The chapter concludes that Downton validates hard honest work as an end in itself, challenging the narcissism of the 'holy You' and expressive individualism.

Walderezak tracks Tom Branson's trajectory from Marxist-quoting socialist chauffeur to estate manager, arguing that the show quietly makes Robert, not Tom, the 'real socialist.' Robert's aristocratic conservatism is read as noblesse oblige (funding the hospital, the Downton Fair, and secretly paying a tenant's arrears), while Matthew's capitalist drive for 'investment, increasing productivity, and reducing waste' is presented as the profit-first ownership system that Marx and Fourier actually criticized. Tom's socialism, closer to the utopian visions of Robert Owen and Charles Fourier than to Marx's class struggle, dissolves as he assimilates into the family ('I haven't abandoned all of my socialism, although sometimes it feels like it'), a capitulation the chapter explains through David Harvey's 'capitalist pacification,' whereby capitalism absorbs all facets of society. The chapter concludes that Robert's treatment of ownership as a duty owed to tenants approaches the cooperative ideals of Fourier and Owen more than Tom's abandoned radicalism ever did.

Wills deploys Georg Simmel's The Philosophy of Money, with its thesis that growing wealth corrodes individuality, to reread Matthew Crawley's courtship of Mary as corruption rather than romance: the man who vows Downton won't change him soon accepts Molesley's valeting, savors finding no grounds to challenge the entail, and returns to the fortune he claimed to renounce. He contrasts their 'relationship of convenience,' which conveniently solves the succession problem, with the penniless Anna and Bates courtship as the show's picture of love uncontaminated by money. The darker claim is that viewers are corrupted alongside Matthew, rooting for a marriage that serves the estate's economic structure, so the show indicts our own captivity to wealth.

Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership versus acceptance or rejection of the social order: the Dowager's 'we don't work' stagnation, Isobel and the Crawley sisters' redemptive projects, Molesley's grateful endurance, and the escapes of Gwen, Alfred, and Branson. The Anna scene, in which she answers her attacker Mr. Green with trained servant courtesy moments after the assault, shows how work 'becomes' us, while the alphabetical ordering of the opening credits suggests that only fulfilling work, not class position, matters. Rousseau, Adam Smith, and Marx frame the negative view of work (agriculture breeding inequality, the pin factory's deadening division of labor, wage exploitation and ideology), against which the chapter endorses Aristotle's pleasures of play and leisure, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper, predicting that automation will soon force everyone to confront what leisure is for.

Dougherty argues that in Downton manners are not incidental etiquette but a central means of demonstrating and cultivating moral character, above all respect for persons, though they can also mask its absence. Matthew's growth from calling valeting 'a very silly occupation' to honoring Molesley's dignity, and Branson's journey from tweed defiance ('uniforms of oppression') to worrying that a tuxedo is insufficient for the Dowager's dinner, show manners tracking their growing respect for the Crawleys as particular individuals. The chapter anchors this in Aristotle's person of visible virtue, Nancy Sherman's 'aesthetic of character,' and Sarah Buss's claim that manners constantly remind us that others are worthy of respect, while Sir Richard's boorishness and the Dowager Countess's weaponized courtesy show manners failing or serving self-interest. Mrs. Crawley's etiquette-breaking kindness, praised even by Violet, complicates the picture by showing care can be morally outrun by propriety.

book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
essays: From the Deserts of Arrakis to the Deserts of Earth
Spice as the Vehicle of Power
The Emergence of Good from Evil
In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . .
samples: Takes the Bene Gesserit Gom Jabbar test as defining humanity as the capacity to endure pain and act for the species rather than chew off one's leg like an animal, reading Paul's habit of walking into traps (Arrakis, the Tleilaxu ghola Hayt in Dune Messiah) and the Atreides ethic of self-sacrifice as passing that test. It ties the Butlerian Jihad's ban on making 'a machine in the likeness of a man's mind' to modern dependence on phones, computers and spell-checkers, echoing Mohiam's claim that removing the crutch 'forced human minds to develop' the two schools of math and politics. With Aristotle it argues that the politics of community and contemplation are the human talents machines atrophy, and ends by casting modern consumers (Harkonnen-like, 250 gallons of water per quarter pounder) as animals caught in a self-made environmental trap.

Argues Herbert populates Dune with three long-running eugenics programs, each with a different ethical stance: the Bene Gesserit's Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (whose communal guardian-breeding deliberately recalls Socrates' Kallipolis in the Republic), Leto II's Golden Path, and the Bene Tleilax's axolotl-tank genetic design for immortality. It reads the chastened Sisterhood of the later novels as moving from consequentialist to Kantian, deontological ground ('never seek to create a human being in any one image'), frames Leto II as the ultimate utilitarian whose species-saving end allegedly justifies Machiavellian means (with Siona's objection that he had no right), and shows the Tleilaxu destroyed by their own monomaniacal religious code. Conclusion: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics.'

Reads Dune through Clausewitz's 'remarkable trinity' of people, military, and government: Duke Leto tries to balance his trinity on Arrakis by winning Fremen support (sending Hawat to negotiate, meeting Stilgar) against Harkonnen sabotage, while Muad'Dib preserves the trinity during the insurgency by bending the Fremen tradition that he duel Stilgar for leadership of Tabr sietch. It argues that once Paul lets messianic myth pull the population element away from his modest political goal of regaining the ducal seat, the trinity falls out of balance and the jihad kills billions, a lesson the author applies to NATO's goal-less war in Afghanistan and post-Saddam Iraq. The upshot: without balance among the three elements and a realistic political goal, war's utility is highly questionable, as Paul's accidental empire shows.

Works through the paradox of foreknowledge: because Paul's Caladan dream of first meeting Chani is knowledge in Plato's justified-true-belief sense, the foreseen future is factive, so his struggle against the jihad he visions (even hoping to die on Feyd-Rautha's blade rather than become a martyr) is futile. It tests the classical escape routes, Boethius's God who views all times as an ever-present eternity and Aquinas's God seeing the whole road 'under the aspect of eternity', and Laplace's Demon's causal determinism, but finds the Atreides oracles unlike God since they are creatures in time who see many possible futures rather than one. The resolution comes through Anscombe's Intention: practical knowledge lets Paul and Leto, whose present choices shift the balance of probability among foreseen timelines, intend their way out as creative authors of events.

Argues that the Fremen, despite their supposed Zensunni faith (which it argues was never a liberation theology), are quintessentially American: Emersonian self-reliance appears as spiritual self-sufficiency and the Spannungsbogen self-imposed delay, while Dewey's democracy as a way of life surfaces in the jihad's aim of replacing master-slave relations with relative equals under Shai-Hulud. It cites Herbert's 'Dune Genesis' on myth-making as pragmatically valuable and reads Paul, who ends Dune Messiah walking blind into the desert 'where we walk without footprints', as kin to the 'American Taliban' John Walker Lindh, whose conversion and jihad were driven by the same self-reliant, spiritual, pragmatic values.

Rejects Herbert's own explanation (hero-worship) for the repeated collapse of Duniverse empires, arguing instead that every ruler from Shaddam IV through Paul and Alia to Leto II governs purely through strategic action, authority enforced by coercion and sanctions, with no democratic legitimacy. Using Habermas's distinction between strategic and communicative action, it reads the Atreides council's evasion of the Landsraad constitution demand, Alia's cry that 'Atreides power must never be marginalized by the chaos of democracy', and Leto II's reliance on breeding programs and deterrence as failures to make the ruled into authors of the law, concluding that physical stability can only last when built on normative stability that democracy provides.

book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
samples: The editors' introduction tells two origin stories for D&D: Gygax and Arneson adapting Tolkien-flavored tabletop wargames like Tactics (the original 1974 subtitle was 'Rules for Fantastic Medieval Wargames Campaigns Playable with Paper and Pencil and Miniature Figures'), versus Gygax's childhood friend Jim Rausch improvising live spy and murder-mystery games where getting 'killed' meant leaving the house. It argues the trouble with classifying what kind of thing D&D is recalls Wittgenstein's claim in Philosophical Investigations that 'game' covers too diverse a range of activities to be defined, echoing Huizinga's Homo Ludens on play lying outside truth and falsehood. The volume's project is announced: stepping back from immersion to ask whether dungeon-crawling is mere escapism or a proving-ground for ideas about morality, metaphysics, and hedonic value.

Littmann recruits Aristotle to answer the charge that D&D is a waste of time: by the function argument the best human life is one of thinking well, and D&D counts even as hack-and-slash, since munchkin optimization and 4e combat roles are logic puzzles, while role-playing is improvisational theater and therefore art. Aristotle's two art-functions are applied to play: catharsis, so that smacking goblins with a mace (his first cleric Brother Silverwolf) purges aggression and fear, and the Poetics' point that poetry explores 'a kind of thing that might be', so a dwarf chieftain losing a son to disintegration or rescuing a thief from stormclaw scorpions makes players reflect on parenthood and what friends owe each other. A good DM, Aristotle-style, keeps events within internal probability (no medusa petrifying someone facing away), players must act in character (the lawful good paladin cannot ride past the bandit-attacked peasant, and 'just playing my character' does not excuse the assassin murdering the magic-user at the inn), yet D&D's fully participatory, player-authored art can still accommodate unaligned and evil PCs.

Merli argues from alignment role-play against Aristotelian virtue ethics: a morally decent player convincingly runs a vicious treacherous thief who frames others for murder, and a 'moral mediocrity' runs a genuinely good paladin, so the ability to judge what the virtuous agent would do is one thing and being virtuous another. This undermines the McDowell/Hursthouse/Jacobson line that only the virtuous, with habituated emotional responses, can 'see what to do' — the role-playing skill works off-line, without feeling the character's fear or sharing its motives, so right-action judgment does not require trained emotion. He adds that if the virtue ethicist retorts that non-virtuous players never really get it right, the contrast between guessing dice in a fist (verifiable success) and claiming to read auras (unverifiable) shows the retort makes virtue look fraudulent, and that role-playing, unlike reading Austen, demands active deliberation from another's point of view, exposing abilities literary examples miss.

Cogburn attacks Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments to five: it deletes archetypes that fantasy literature needs, since Karsa Orlong (who wills the destruction of all civilization without sadism) and Jacqueline Carey's Haomane Firstborn (who loves cold mathematical order while his laws lead to genocide) fit nowhere in the new scheme. He rebuilds alignment by taking it to describe what a character wills in Kant's sense, mapping the law-chaos axis onto the categorical imperative (the liar and murderer must take themselves to be exceptions to universal laws) and the good-evil axis onto Mill's greatest happiness principle, which yields a Lawful Good of Gandhi and King, a Neutral Good modeled on Jesus breaking Sabbath law out of love, and Lawful Evil exemplified by vampire hierarchies and politicians whose policies create hell abroad. Joe Abercrombie's torturer San Dan Glotka becomes the archetypal Neutral Neutral, 'banality of evil' in Arendt's sense, and the chapter concludes Chaotic Good is empty because willing the destruction of universalizability cannot consistently will less pain.

Bateman replies to Cogburn by recovering the alignment system's actual literary source: Moorcock's Elric saga, where Law and Chaos are rival political ideologies (conservative and liberal tendencies) held in check by the Cosmic Balance, so a Chaotic person need only refuse law's authority, not will horror, and Chaotic Good remains possible. He rejects Cogburn's 'sausage machine' reading of Kant's first formula in favor of the humanity formula and the Realm of Ends, and rejects act utilitarianism as a model of the Good alignment, since an overpopulation scenario shows Mill's calculus mandating culling-genocide and Bentham's felicific calculus cannot actually measure goodness. Drawing on Badiou's ethic of truths, Buddhist and Jain renunciation, and the true-Neutral Druid as servant of the Cosmic Balance, he argues neutrality between Good and Evil need not be monstrous and mourns 4e's 'childishly simplistic' new system.

Silcox's fifth-level paladin died to eighty-three orcs and his middle-school friends held a funeral, and the chapter asks whether grief for a PC death is rational. Charles Taylor's narrative ethics — we grasp our lives as unfolding stories — would vindicate it, but objections from Beckett's Waiting for Godot and MacEwan's Atonement (via critic Samantha Vice) show stories can discourage seeing life as narrative, and the decisive asymmetry is Nagel's point about death: after the paladin falls the campaign story continues and the player can still watch it, whereas a person's own death forecloses any finding out how things turn out, a difference like February cold versus interstellar cold. He proposes instead that the self is a 'back-story' or metanarrative precondition of storytelling, closing against Descartes' Meditations claim that the power of imagination is 'in no way necessary' to his essence — take away someone's capacity for shared fiction entirely and nothing recognizable remains.

book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
samples: The book's introduction explains how Card's novel grew out of his childhood fascination with Asimov's Foundation and its 'psychohistory,' and why the premise of a monitored 'Third' child socially engineered by Colonel Graff into a child commander attracts such diverse readers, including real military trainees who identify with Ender. It previews the volume's five parts: Ender's education and moral making, the philosophy of war games and empathy, the buggers as misunderstood others, the ethics of xenocide and wartime responsibility, and the postwar nets politics of Locke, Demosthenes, and the Hegemon.

Cam Cobb pits Socratic critical inquiry and Plato's Republic-style vocational streaming (classes sorted by the 'myth of the metals,' sold through a noble lie) against the Battle School curriculum, which is almost purely vocational and lacks the music, poetry, and liberal paideia that harmonize the soul. Testing Socrates' dialogic method, Dewey's aptitude-tracking education, and Freire's problem-posing alternative against the battleroom, the Giant's Drink, and Graff's secretly rewritten game rules, Cobb concludes Ender's schooling mixes conflicting pedagogies and ends in the teacher domination Freire feared, crystallized in Ender's lament 'I've spent my life as someone's pawn.'

Jeremy Proulx reads Ender's refrain 'I didn't want to hurt him!' through Schelling's account of evil as a real 'contraction into the self' rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: the beatings of Stilson, the boy on the shuttle, Bonzo, and the Giant reveal a Peter-like monstrosity in Ender that he can neither understand nor control. Graff's engineered isolation forces Ender to confront this dark ground, and his moral development culminates in Valentine's 'Welcome to the human race' — the recognition that freedom is tainted by a necessity we do not choose, so Ender stays responsible for xenocide even though he was tricked.

Jeff Ewing asks which moral theory governs the novel, finding deontology absent and a contest between Graff's utilitarian recruiting pitch and a virtue-ethical focus on character: the I.F. allowed a 'Third' because it wanted Ender's traits rather than his acts. Mapping Plato's cardinal virtues and tripartite-soul politics against Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, he argues Ender's minimum-force self-defense, adaptability, and disregard for hierarchy are Aristotelian virtues, while his killings of Stilson, Bonzo, and the buggers fall outside the mean only because he lacked the intellectual virtue of grasping his full situation.

Chad Timm reads Battle School through Foucault's disciplinary power: monitors in the skull, sorting into armies, minute-by-minute schedules, and constant testing are the power/knowledge that constructs 'the soldier,' while the ever-possible observation of teachers and desks makes the school Bentham's Panopticon that trains students to police themselves. The proof of Ender's constructed identity is his singling out of Bean exactly as Graff singled him out on the shuttle, and Timm extends the lesson to standardized testing and Obama's 'Race to the Top.'

Andrew Zimmerman Jones treats Ender's conflicts as games analyzable by von Neumann's minimax theorem and the theory of zero-sum, imperfect-information games, arguing Ender wins by redefining the game itself ('the enemy's gate is down') while his empathy fails only with Graff, whose larger game Ender never suspects because he never treats the adults as the enemy. He unpacks Ender's claim that to understand an enemy is to love him through Socrates' words in Plato's Laches on courage, Hume's account of sympathy, and the Christian agape of 'love your enemies,' mapping a continuum from sympathy through empathy to love.

book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness
essays: Howl at the Moon If You Want To
“Doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing”
It’s Life in the Solar System, Jim, But Not as We Know It
The Burden of the End of the World
samples: James S. A. Corey (Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck) frame both philosophy and science fiction as 'acts of critical imagination': philosophy advances into questions before data and measurement exist, and science fiction imagines what we do not yet know until it stops being speculative. They describe The Expanse as a collaborative project built from the science fiction they read growing up (Bester, Niven, Clarke, Cherryh) and from real history, its boundaries clear only at a distance. The foreword presents this volume as the conversation they inherited carrying forward, with The Expanse as touchstone, hoping it leaves readers 'a little more awed, a little wiser.'

Editor Jeffery L. Nicholas declares Leviathan Wakes 'that book' and the TV series 'that show' of philosophical science fiction, and explains that his own aphantasia makes the series especially precious to him (watching the Rocinante on screen, Naomi's torture to save lives). He frames the volume's guiding questions over the first five seasons with hints from Babylon's Ashes: whether Amos or Avasarala is more evil and Naomi or Holden good, the costs of interstellar migration through the Ring Gates, and whether humanity even has a choice about expansion. Like Joe Miller holding Julie's necklace, the contributors offer their love of the show through interrogation of Miller, Holden, Amos, Bobbie, Naomi, and Avasarala herself.

Michael J. O'Neill argues that infinite space is The Expanse's most constant on-screen character, conveyed through chiaroscuro cinematography that deliberately echoes the seventeenth century (the Don Quixote references, 'Dulcinea', the Rocinante's name), when humanity first confronted infinite space. He reads Pascal's terror at man as 'a middle point between all and nothing' into Avasarala's losing debate with Nancy Gao over the Ring gold rush and into Miller's agoraphobic quest for Julie, then contrasts this with Kant's mathematically and dynamically sublime: spacewalks, the Behemoth dwarfed at the Gate, the Arboghast disassembled over Venus, and Inaros' asteroid attack as the weaponization of the infinite. Against Pascal's insignificance, Kant's sublime reveals our freedom — Holden's 'crazy notion about free will' while descending to the Ring station, Drummer's 'nothing in the void is foreign to us', and Amos' 'we're still here' — so the awe the show's visuals provoke is an intuition that we are greater than all nature's power.

Margarida Hermida deploys Parfit's comparison of peace, a war killing 99 percent of humanity, and one killing everyone to argue extinction is categorically worse than mass death, and makes the stakes concrete through The Expanse's threats: the protomolecule, all-out Earth-Mars-Belt war, and the Free Navy's asteroid attack that kills billions. She rejects Miller's 'stars are better off without us' pessimism by arguing human existence is a good when suffering is fought (Belter disease and Ceres trafficking are contingent injustices, not necessities), values humanity as the only species with civilization and as the universe 'starting to understand itself', and distinguishes the desirable biological colonization of lifeless worlds from the protomolecule makers' morally objectionable disregard for native life like Ilus'. Against Phil Torres' worry that human speciation means endless war, she points to the mixed Rocinante crew and Naomi's line that the real divide is 'people who want more violence and the ones who want less', concluding with Parfit's On What Matters that what matters most is avoiding the end of human history and of rational beings.

Leonard Kahn takes the season-four debate between Avasarala and Nancy Gao over Ring colonization and asks who should have won. Using Parfit's extinction asymmetry, Bostrom's 'astronomical waste', and Toby Ord's definition of existential risk, he calculates that the 1,300 Ring gates could make accessible between 10^34 and 10^71 future lives (versus the Epstein-drive Nauvoo's century-long crawl to Tau Ceti), yet because using the rings risks the annihilation that befell the protomolecule's creators, the loss of humanity's long-term potential outweighs Gao's 'unimaginable opportunities' — so Avasarala's caution should have won. He ends skeptically: like Socrates arguing against the execution of the Arginusae generals, philosophical Cassandras rarely prevail, Gao was probably right that ring colonization was politically inevitable, and we face the same dilemma with nuclear war, engineered pandemics, and runaway AI.

S. W. Sondheimer argues that Avasarala's election loss to Nancy Gao is explained not by competence but by millennia of gender expectations. She excavates the lineage: Aristotle's form/matter hierarchy ('matter yearns for form as the female for the male', women as incomplete 'deformed males' with 'fewer teeth') used to bar women from politics, Hume's portrait of women as near-livestock incapable of the sublime, and Romantic-era bodily confinement — mapping each onto Avasarala's staff recasting her as a 'nurturing, caring family matriarch', her forced public apology for the failed Inaros boarding raid that a male commander like Errinwright would never have had to make, and Arjun seizing control of the narrative of their son Charanpal's death. Closing the loop with the 2016 US election (Clinton versus Trump), the chapter argues that even in 2350 voters punish the 'nasty woman' and reward the comfortable mold Gao fits, and demands we 'dig this garbage philosophy out of our shared consciousness and set it on fire.'

book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
essays: Flesh Is Weak, but Questions Endure
samples: The editors' introduction recounts how Fallout overcame early adaptation jitters (Bethesda's Peter Hines warned in 2015 that more could go wrong than right in a screen version) because the games' blank overworld maps and faction-defining choices, from the original water-chip quest to New Vegas's player-decided ending, invite wondering about everyone else's story in the wastes. It argues that this world-building raises genuinely philosophical questions - why we are drawn to fictional atrocities, whether wasteland life is too bad to bring children into, whether ghouls and synths are persons, and what makes anything right or wrong - and presents the book's essays as attempts to raise, clarify, and answer them.

Mackenzie Graham uses Fallout 3's Project Purity - James's sacrificial death and the Lone Wanderer's choice among feeding the purifier with their own life, poisoning the water for the Enclave, or destroying it - to ask whether death and posthumous events can be bad for the one who dies. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, the chapter defends deprivationism with the Megaton quest (the Lone Wanderer's desire to save the town is thwarted even if the rearmed bomb destroys it unbeknownst to them) and weighs Feinberg and Pitcher's ante-mortem person against the problem of the subject, using the Great War's redefinition of October 22, 2077 to block backward causation. The 'Blood Ties' quest with the Family's cannibals then raises posthumous wrongs: since no existing subject is harmed or wronged, the chapter ends by asking whether cannibalism is an impersonal wrong against personhood itself, on the model of respecting nature.

Eric Silverman asks whether the Amazon series' Lucy and Maximus should have children, framing the wasteland through Hobbes's state of nature where life is 'nasty, brutish, and short' and even vaults are limiting experiments. He lays out Benatar's Harm Argument (pain outweighs pleasure, so procreation is procreational Russian roulette) and Shiffrin's Consent Argument (no one consents to being born, as Sartre's 'I did not ask to be born' concedes), then rebuts them: Socrates, the Stoics, and Aristotle make virtue and meaning rather than pleasure the goal of life, so a harsh wasteland full of people needing help suits a virtuous, sacrificial life like the hero's exile at the end of the original Fallout. Parental proxy consent legitimizes procreation as it does children's medical decisions, and Kant's universalization test defeats the demand for pre-natal consent, since universalizing it would eliminate the very rational beings whose consent it protects - so Lucy's 'Okey dokey!' optimism wins.

David Lawrence opens with Fallout 4's 'Blind Betrayal', where Elder Maxson orders the player to execute Paladin Danse once his synth origin is revealed, and argues that moral status is a matter of capacities - sense of self, notion of past and future, values, life-plans, moral agency - drawing on Charles Taylor's concept of a person and narrative identity, not on biological substrate. Nick Valentine's hunt for Eddie Winter in 'Long Time Coming' and Curie's chosen embodiment in 'Emergent Behavior' show machines weaving reconstructed pasts into new life-plans, while ghouls like Hancock and Raul ('Old School Ghoul') and super mutants like Fawkes (who refuses to enter the lethal radiation chamber: 'I would not rob you of that') and the community-builder Marcus prove branded monsters can be more human than human. The factions embody warring philosophies of moral status: the Institute's property-slavery of its creations, the Brotherhood's 'wisdom of repugnance' (Leon Kass), and the Railroad's capacity-based abolitionism, with DiMA's Far Harbor question - how do you know you are not a synth? - turning the issue on the player.

Trevor Hedberg asks whether 'Kill Everything' playthroughs of New Vegas are wrong, from the Goodsprings opening (where the player may massacre both Powder Gangers and settlers) to installing a mod that makes Freeside's unkillable children killable. He rejects the empirical aggression argument (the evidence is mixed and effects tiny, and alcohol or contact sports set a precedent) and the Kantian disrespect argument, since Fallout's NPCs - stuck on terrain, repeating dialogue - lack the rational agency the Humanity Formulation protects. The best case against virtual slaughter is Aristotle's virtue ethics: courage as the mean between recklessness and cowardice, eudaimonia as activity in accord with virtue, so the morality of playing turns on motives - exploring narratives or seeking combat challenge can be innocent, but killing for the pleasure of settlers' horrified flight corrodes character.

The Funkes apply Clark and Chalmers's extended mind hypothesis to the Pip-Boy, arguing it meets all three criteria for cognitive extension - availability (worn at all times), reliability (trusted rad and health monitoring), and active cognitive engagement (V.A.T.S. offloads targeting calculations) - so it is part of the Sole Survivor's and Courier's minds, as in 'The Glowing Sea' and the search for Virgil's cure. Donna Haraway's cyborg frames this human-machine hybridity alongside cyberdogs and Kellogg, but Fallout inverts her liberationist vision: the Pip-Boy is a survival lifeline forced by the wasteland, not an emancipatory choice, making the cyborg a dystopian necessity. Comparing the Pip-Boy with cochlear implants, prosthetics, and brain-computer interfaces, and the Old World Blues Think Tank with a dehumanizing bio-tech extreme, the chapter uses Alison Kafer's feminist crip critique to insist real augmentation carries pain, stigma, and unequal access the game's frictionless fiction erases, closing on a cautious transhumanist note.
